eras.title: Key Topic 1: The Development of the Civil Rights Movement, 1954–60
Key Topic 2: Protest, Progress and Radicalism, 1960–75
Key Topic 3: US Involvement in the Vietnam War, 1954–75
Key Topic 4: Reactions to, and the End of, US Involvement in Vietnam, 1964–75

milestones.title: Southern Jim Crow Segregation, Voter Barriers & Work of NAACP and CORE
milestones.specTag: KT 1.1 • Position of Black Americans in the Early 1950s
milestones.enquiryQuestion: How did Jim Crow laws enforce Southern segregation—and how did NAACP and CORE challenge them?
milestones.imageCaption: Everyday Jim Crow segregation at a Southern railway station drinking fountain marked 'Colored'.
milestones.mapCaption: Reference Map: De jure Jim Crow segregation across 17 Southern states and Washington D.C. versus Northern de facto discrimination.
milestones.catalyst: Protected by the 1896 ***Plessy v. Ferguson*** ('separate but equal') ruling, **17 Southern states** enforced **de jure Jim Crow** laws across schools, buses, and waiting rooms while **literacy tests, poll taxes**, and terror barred Black voters.
milestones.turningPoint: Returning WWII veterans (**Double V Campaign**) swelled **NAACP** membership (~500,000), whose Legal Defense Fund under **Thurgood Marshall** challenged unequal education in federal courts while **CORE** (founded 1942) pioneered interracial sit-ins.
milestones.impact: Laid the twin legal and non-violent grassroots foundations of the civil rights movement, culminating in the NAACP's consolidated five-state school lawsuit before the Supreme Court.
milestones.bridgeToNext: Thurgood Marshall's courtroom strategy reached its decisive constitutional breakthrough at the Supreme Court on 17 May 1954.

keyTerms.definition: Southern state segregation laws upheld by the 1896 Supreme Court doctrine claiming 'separate but equal' facilities were constitutional.
Discriminatory Southern fees and rigged constitutional exams used by white registrars to disenfranchise Black citizens.
Leading civil rights groups combining NAACP federal court litigation (1909) with CORE's non-violent direct action (1942).

milestones.title: Brown v. Board of Education of Topeka: Overturning ‘Separate but Equal’
milestones.specTag: KT 1.2 • Causes, Features & Impact of Brown v. Topeka (1954)
milestones.enquiryQuestion: Why was the unanimous May 1954 Brown v. Topeka ruling a legal turning point—and what limited it?
milestones.imageCaption: Chief Justice Earl Warren (seated centre) and the US Supreme Court justices who delivered the unanimous 9–0 Brown ruling in May 1954.
milestones.mapCaption: Reference Map: Mandatory school segregation across 17 Southern states on the eve of Brown v. Board of Education (1954).
milestones.catalyst: Oliver Brown sued Topeka's school board so his daughter Linda could attend a nearby white elementary school; **Thurgood Marshall** cited the **14th Amendment** and Kenneth and Mamie Clark's **doll tests**.
milestones.turningPoint: On **17 May 1954**, **Chief Justice Earl Warren** delivered a unanimous **9–0 Supreme Court verdict** declaring *'separate educational facilities are inherently unequal'*, followed by **Brown II (May 1955)** ordering integration with *'all deliberate speed'*.
milestones.impact: Q3d Core Debate: **Landmark Legal Victory** shattered *Plessy*'s constitutional shield and inspired Black optimism, whereas **Practical Limits** notes *'all deliberate speed'* had no deadline—leaving **<2% of Deep South Black children** in integrated schools by 1957.
milestones.bridgeToNext: The very same month *Brown* struck down school segregation at home, French colonial collapse at Dien Bien Phu drew Eisenhower into Vietnam abroad.

keyTerms.definition: Unanimous 9–0 Supreme Court decision overturning Plessy v. Ferguson in public education under the 14th Amendment.
May 1955 follow-up Supreme Court order omitting a fixed deadline, exploited by Southern school boards to stall integration.

milestones.title: Dien Bien Phu, The 1954 Geneva Accords & Eisenhower’s Domino Theory
milestones.specTag: KT 3.1 • Reasons for Early US Involvement in Vietnam under Eisenhower
milestones.enquiryQuestion: Why did French defeat in 1954 pull President Eisenhower into backing South Vietnam?
milestones.imageCaption: Delegates at the July 1954 Geneva Conference dividing Vietnam temporarily along the 17th Parallel.
milestones.mapCaption: Reference Map: Partition of Vietnam at the 17th Parallel DMZ (July 1954) between Communist North Vietnam and US-backed South Vietnam.
milestones.catalyst: Despite US funding 80% of France's war costs, **Ho Chi Minh** and **General Giap**'s Viet Minh crushed French forces at **Dien Bien Phu (May 1954)** amid Cold War fears of Chinese and Soviet expansion.
milestones.turningPoint: The **July 1954 Geneva Accords** divided Vietnam temporarily along the **17th Parallel** pending 1956 elections; proclaiming **the domino theory**, **President Eisenhower** refused to sign Geneva, formed **SEATO**, and sent money and military advisers to Saigon.
milestones.impact: Locked Washington into preserving a non-communist South Vietnam as a Cold War test of containment, blinding US policymakers to Vietnamese anti-colonial nationalism.
milestones.bridgeToNext: Back across the American South in 1954–55, white segregationists answered the *Brown* verdict with economic reprisals and shocking racial murder.
keyAgents: Ho Chi Minh & General Vo Nguyen Giap

keyTerms.definition: Peace settlement ending French rule in Indochina and dividing Vietnam at the 17th Parallel until nationwide elections scheduled for 1956.
Eisenhower's belief that if South Vietnam fell to communism, neighbouring Laos, Cambodia, Thailand, and Malaya would topple in turn.

milestones.title: White Citizens’ Councils, KKK Terror & The Murder of Emmett Till
milestones.specTag: KT 1.4 • KKK Violence, Murder of Emmet Till (1955) & Southern Opposition
milestones.enquiryQuestion: How did White Citizens' Councils, Dixiecrats, and Emmett Till's murder expose Southern resistance?
milestones.imageCaption: Mamie Till-Mobley grieving at her 14-year-old son Emmett Till's funeral in September 1955 after insisting on an open casket.
milestones.mapCaption: Reference Map: Deep South centres of White Citizens' Council economic intimidation and KKK violence.
milestones.catalyst: Outraged by *Brown*, Southern business elites formed **White Citizens' Councils** (from July 1954) to fire and evict Black petitioners, **'Dixiecrats'** signed the **1956 Southern Manifesto** (101 congressmen), and **Ku Klux Klan** bombings surged.
milestones.turningPoint: In **August 1955**, 14-year-old Chicago schoolboy **Emmett Till** (*Emmet Till*) was abducted and murdered in Money, Mississippi by Roy Bryant and J.W. Milam; **Mamie Till-Mobley's open-casket funeral** (*Jet* photos) shocked the world before an **all-white jury acquitted** the killers in 67 minutes.
milestones.impact: Exposed the total corruption of Jim Crow courts when Bryant and Milam confessed for $4,000 in *Look* magazine—galvanising Rosa Parks and a generation of young activists just 100 days later.
milestones.bridgeToNext: That autumn on the other side of the globe, US-backed strongman Ngo Dinh Diem rigged a referendum in Saigon and blocked Vietnam's 1956 elections.

keyTerms.definition: 'Uptown Klan' of white bankers, employers, and officials formed in July 1954 using job sackings, evictions, and credit bans to block integration.
Brutal Mississippi lynching of 14-year-old Emmett Till whose open-casket photographs and all-white jury acquittal outraged national opinion.
Southern Democratic lawmakers who signed the March 1956 manifesto pledging 'Massive Resistance' to federal desegregation.

milestones.title: Ngo Dinh Diem’s Rigged Referendum & Cancelled 1956 Reunification Vote
milestones.specTag: KT 3.1 • Weaknesses of the Diem Government & US Backing
milestones.enquiryQuestion: Why did Eisenhower back Ngo Dinh Diem despite corruption, nepotism, and cancelled elections?
milestones.imageCaption: South Vietnamese President Ngo Dinh Diem welcomed by President Dwight D. Eisenhower on an official state visit in May 1957.
milestones.catalyst: Knowing **Ho Chi Minh** would win roughly 80% of a free national vote, Washington backed fervently anti-communist Catholic **Ngo Dinh Diem** as South Vietnam's leader.
milestones.turningPoint: In **October 1955**, Diem ousted Emperor Bao Dai via a **rigged referendum (98.2% vote**, more ballots in Saigon than voters), proclaimed the Republic of Vietnam, and **cancelled the July 1956 Geneva elections** while receiving **$1.6bn+** in US aid and ~900 advisers.
milestones.impact: Prevented peaceful Communist reunification in 1956, yet Diem's **Catholic nepotism**, landlord land seizures, and repression of the **Buddhist peasant majority** made Saigon deeply unpopular.
milestones.bridgeToNext: Meanwhile in Montgomery, Alabama on 1 December 1955, Rosa Parks refused to surrender her bus seat—launching 381 days of mass non-violent protest.
keyAgents: Ho Chi Minh & General Vo Nguyen Giap

keyTerms.definition: US-backed Catholic President of South Vietnam (1955–63) whose nepotism, rigged ballots, and anti-Buddhist policies alienated rural peasants.
Diem's US-supported refusal to hold the nationwide reunification vote promised at Geneva lest Ho Chi Minh win peacefully.

milestones.title: Rosa Parks, Martin Luther King Jr., The 381-Day Boycott & SCLC
milestones.specTag: KT 1.3 • Montgomery Bus Boycott, Browder v. Gayle & Founding SCLC
milestones.enquiryQuestion: Why did the 1955–56 Montgomery Bus Boycott succeed in ending bus segregation?
milestones.imageCaption: NAACP secretary Rosa Parks arriving at court in Montgomery with E.D. Nixon on 5 December 1955 as the citywide bus boycott began.
milestones.catalyst: After NAACP activist **Rosa Parks** was arrested on **1 December 1955** for refusing to give up her Montgomery bus seat, **Jo Ann Robinson**'s **Women's Political Council** distributed 35,000 boycott leaflets overnight.
milestones.turningPoint: Electing 26-year-old **Dr Martin Luther King Jr.** president of the **MIA**, **40,000 Black residents** sustained a **381-day boycott** via a **300-car pool** (slashing bus revenue by 65%) until the Supreme Court ruled bus segregation unconstitutional in ***Browder v. Gayle* (Nov 1956)**; King founded the **SCLC (Jan 1957)**.
milestones.impact: Q3d Core Debate: **Grassroots Direct Action & King** stresses mass Black discipline, WPC/church organisation, and King's non-violent oratory, whereas **Federal Courts** notes Montgomery officials never yielded until *Browder v. Gayle* forced integration.
milestones.bridgeToNext: Nine months after Montgomery's buses integrated, Arkansas Governor Orval Faubus triggered a constitutional showdown over school integration at Little Rock.

keyTerms.definition: Coalition of Black ministers and community leaders (MIA) formed on 5 December 1955 under Martin Luther King Jr. to run the 381-day boycott.
Supreme Court ruling affirming that segregated seating on Montgomery public buses violated the 14th Amendment.
Southern Christian Leadership Conference co-founded by Martin Luther King Jr. to coordinate church-led non-violent protests across the South.

milestones.title: Events at Little Rock High School & The Civil Rights Act (1957)
milestones.specTag: KT 1.2–1.3 • Little Rock (1957), Federal Troops & 1957 Civil Rights Act
milestones.enquiryQuestion: Why did Eisenhower send the 101st Airborne to Little Rock in September 1957?
milestones.imageCaption: Fifteen-year-old Elizabeth Eckford walking calmly past a jeering white mob outside Little Rock Central High School on 4 September 1957.
milestones.catalyst: Defying a federal court desegregation plan in **September 1957**, Arkansas **Governor Orval Faubus** deployed the **Arkansas National Guard** to block the **Little Rock Nine** (including **Elizabeth Eckford**) before global TV cameras.
milestones.turningPoint: To uphold federal authority and Cold War prestige, **President Eisenhower** signed the watered-down **Civil Rights Act (9 Sept 1957)** and on **24 September** federalised the Guard and sent **1,000 paratroopers of the 101st Airborne** to escort the students (before ***Cooper v. Aaron*** ended Faubus's 1958–59 'Lost Year' school closure).
milestones.impact: Proved the White House would use military force against defiant state governors, though Dixiecrat filibusters (Strom Thurmond) gutted the **1957 Act** so Black voter registration rose **under 3%** by 1960.
milestones.bridgeToNext: Impatient at glacial courtroom and legislative progress by 1960, Black college students in North Carolina took direct action into their own hands.
keyAgents: Elizabeth Eckford & The Little Rock Nine

keyTerms.definition: Nine Black teenagers chosen on merit to integrate Little Rock Central High School under 101st Airborne protection.
First federal civil rights law since 1875 creating a Civil Rights Commission, heavily weakened by Dixiecrat jury-trial amendments.
Faubus's 1958–59 closure of all Little Rock high schools, struck down by the Supreme Court ordering integrated reopening.

milestones.title: The Greensboro Woolworth Sit-Ins & Founding of SNCC
milestones.specTag: KT 2.1 • Significance of Greensboro & the Sit-In Movement (1960)
milestones.enquiryQuestion: How did four freshmen at Greensboro revitalise the civil rights movement in 1960?
milestones.imageCaption: The Greensboro Four—Ezell Blair Jr., Franklin McCain, Joseph McNeill, and David Richmond—outside Woolworth's in February 1960.
milestones.mapCaption: Reference Map: Rapid spread of student lunch-counter sit-ins across the South (1960) and CORE's 1961 Freedom Ride routes.
milestones.catalyst: Frustrated that six years after *Brown* downtown stores took Black shoppers' money yet barred them from lunch counters, four Black students (**the Greensboro Four**) sat at an all-white **Woolworth's** counter on **1 February 1960**.
milestones.turningPoint: Within months **70,000+ Black and white students** staged disciplined non-violent **sit-ins, kneel-ins, and wade-ins** across 55+ cities, while veteran organiser **Ella Baker** helped students found **SNCC** at Raleigh in **April 1960**.
milestones.impact: Desegregated Woolworth's (July 1960) and lunch counters in **100+ cities**, proved grassroots youth protest could hit white business profits fast, and created **SNCC** as a fearless frontline organising force.
milestones.bridgeToNext: As student activism surged in America in late 1960, peasant anger against Diem in South Vietnam gave birth to an armed revolutionary movement.

keyTerms.definition: Woolworth's lunch-counter protest begun by four North Carolina A&T students that sparked a mass youth sit-in movement.
Student Nonviolent Coordinating Committee founded with Ella Baker's guidance to run grassroots direct action and voter drives.

milestones.title: Diem’s Rural Repression, Founding of the Vietcong & Kennedy’s Advisers
milestones.specTag: KT 3.1 • Diem's Weaknesses & Greater Involvement under Kennedy
milestones.enquiryQuestion: How did Diem's rural repression trigger the Vietcong insurgency and Kennedy's escalation?
milestones.imageCaption: Guerrilla fighters of the National Liberation Front (Vietcong), formed in South Vietnam in December 1960 to overthrow Ngo Dinh Diem.
milestones.mapCaption: Reference Map: The 17th Parallel DMZ and the Ho Chi Minh Trail jungle supply network running through Laos and Cambodia.
milestones.catalyst: Diem's corrupt landlord policies, abolition of elected village councils, and arrest/execution of **40,000+ suspected dissidents** alienated South Vietnam's Buddhist peasantry.
milestones.turningPoint: In **December 1960**, southern opponents formed the **National Liberation Front (Vietcong / VC)** supplied by North Vietnam along the **Ho Chi Minh Trail**; incoming **President John F. Kennedy** expanded US military advisers from **~900 to 16,000+** by 1963.
milestones.impact: Turned South Vietnam into an expanding guerrilla war where Vietcong fighters won peasant support through land reform while US-supplied **ARVN** troops suffered low morale.
milestones.bridgeToNext: In May 1961, Kennedy faced an immediate domestic crisis when Ku Klux Klan mobs firebombed interracial Freedom Riders in Alabama.
keyAgents: Ho Chi Minh & General Vo Nguyen Giap

keyTerms.definition: National Liberation Front of South Vietnam—Communist-led guerrilla force fighting to topple Diem and reunify Vietnam.
Concealed jungle supply network running from North Vietnam through neutral Laos and Cambodia to arm the Vietcong.

milestones.title: CORE’s Freedom Riders, The Anniston Bomb (1961) & The James Meredith Case (1962)
milestones.specTag: KT 2.1 • Freedom Riders, KKK Violence & James Meredith (1961–62)
milestones.enquiryQuestion: How did Klan violence against Freedom Riders and James Meredith force Kennedy to act?
milestones.imageCaption: Smoke billowing from the firebombed Greyhound Freedom Rider bus ambushed by the Ku Klux Klan outside Anniston, Alabama on 14 May 1961.
milestones.mapCaption: Reference Map: The May 1961 Freedom Rides from Washington D.C. through Anniston, Birmingham, Montgomery, and Jackson, Mississippi.
milestones.catalyst: **CORE** (James Farmer) and **SNCC** launched interracial **Freedom Rides (May 1961)** to test whether Deep South states obeyed ***Boynton v. Virginia* (1960)** outlawing segregated interstate bus terminals.
milestones.turningPoint: **Ku Klux Klan** mobs firebombed a bus at **Anniston (14 May 1961)** and beat riders in Montgomery, forcing **Robert Kennedy** to send **500+ federal marshals** and enforce **ICC terminal desegregation (Nov 1961)**; in **Oct 1962**, JFK sent troops so **James Meredith** could enrol at the University of Mississippi.
milestones.impact: Proved violent Southern defiance (*Governor Ross Barnett* at 'Ole Miss', leaving 2 dead) repeatedly compelled a cautious Kennedy administration to enforce federal civil rights rulings.
milestones.bridgeToNext: Seeing federal action followed televised white brutality, Martin Luther King Jr. targeted Bull Connor's Birmingham in spring 1963.

keyTerms.definition: May 1961 interracial bus rides attacked by KKK firebombers in Anniston, Alabama, compelling ICC enforcement of terminal desegregation.
Black Air Force veteran whose court-ordered admission to the segregated University of Mississippi required federal marshals and troops.

milestones.title: King’s Peace Marches in Birmingham & The March on Washington (1963)
milestones.specTag: KT 2.2 • Peaceful Protests of 1963 in Birmingham & Washington
milestones.enquiryQuestion: How did Birmingham's Children's Crusade and the March on Washington transform national opinion?
milestones.imageCaption: Police attack dogs set upon peaceful civil rights demonstrators under Eugene 'Bull' Connor during Project C in Birmingham, May 1963.
milestones.catalyst: After the unsuccessful Albany campaign, **King** and the **SCLC** launched **Project C** in **Birmingham, Alabama ('Bombingham', April 1963)**, where King penned his *Letter from Birmingham Jail*.
milestones.turningPoint: In May 1963, **Eugene 'Bull' Connor** unleashed **police dogs and high-pressure fire hoses** on schoolchildren (**Children's Crusade**) on global TV, prompting JFK to draft a Civil Rights Bill; on **28 August 1963**, **250,000** marched on **Washington** for King's ***'I Have a Dream'*** speech.
milestones.impact: Turned civil rights into an urgent moral crisis for white America and Congress—further galvanized in **September 1963** when a KKK bomb at Birmingham's **16th Street Baptist Church** killed four Black girls.
milestones.bridgeToNext: That same summer and autumn of 1963, Buddhist monk self-immolations in Saigon destroyed US faith in Diem's South Vietnamese regime.

keyTerms.definition: May 1963 SCLC Birmingham marches where Bull Connor's dogs and fire hoses against schoolchildren shocked televised audiences worldwide.
Peaceful interracial rally of 250,000 at the Lincoln Memorial demanding jobs and JFK's Civil Rights Bill, climaxing in 'I Have a Dream'.

milestones.title: Failure of the Strategic Hamlet Program, Buddhist Crisis & Overthrow of Diem
milestones.specTag: KT 3.1 • Kennedy's Involvement: Strategic Hamlets & Overthrow of Diem
milestones.enquiryQuestion: Why did the Strategic Hamlet Program backfire and lead to Diem's overthrow in November 1963?
milestones.imageCaption: Buddhist monk Thich Quang Duc burning himself to death in Saigon in June 1963 to protest Ngo Dinh Diem's persecution of Buddhists.
milestones.catalyst: Launched by Kennedy and Diem in **1962**, the **Strategic Hamlet Program** forcibly uprooted **4m+ rural peasants** from ancestral graves into barbed-wire villages—driving furious farmers straight into **Vietcong** ranks.
milestones.turningPoint: After Diem's troops shot Buddhist protesters in Hue and monk **Thich Quang Duc** burned himself alive in Saigon (**June 1963**), Washington signalled it would not block an **ARVN generals' coup**, which toppled and **assassinated Diem on 1–2 November 1963** (three weeks before JFK's own assassination).
milestones.impact: Rather than stabilising Saigon, Diem's murder unleashed **ten chaotic military juntas in 18 months**, letting the Vietcong seize **~40% of rural South Vietnam** by 1964 and deepening US responsibility.
milestones.bridgeToNext: Succeeding assassinated President Kennedy in November 1963, Lyndon B. Johnson faced twin turning points in summer 1964: passing the Civil Rights Act and confronting North Vietnam.

keyTerms.definition: Failed US-Saigon counter-insurgency scheme herding rural villagers behind barbed wire to isolate them from Vietcong guerrillas.
Anti-Diem protests sparked by Thich Quang Duc's June 1963 self-immolation, ending in the CIA-tolerated November 1963 ARVN coup.

milestones.title: Freedom Summer Murders & Passage of the Civil Rights Act (1964)
milestones.specTag: KT 2.2 • Freedom Summer, Mississippi Murders & Civil Rights Act (1964)
milestones.enquiryQuestion: How did peaceful protest and Presidential skill pass the landmark Civil Rights Act of 1964?
milestones.imageCaption: President Lyndon B. Johnson signing the Civil Rights Act of 1964 on 2 July 1964 with Dr Martin Luther King Jr. standing behind him.
milestones.catalyst: While **SNCC and CORE** volunteers entered Mississippi during **June 1964 Freedom Summer**—where Klansmen murdered civil rights workers **Chaney, Goodman, and Schwerner**—**President Lyndon B. Johnson** invoked JFK's memory to break a 54-day Southern Senate filibuster.
milestones.turningPoint: Signed into law on **2 July 1964**, the **Civil Rights Act (1964)** outlawed segregation in all public accommodations (hotels, restaurants, theatres), empowered federal funding cuts to segregated schools, and created the **EEOC** against workplace discrimination.
milestones.impact: Q3d Core Debate: **Presidential Mastery** credits LBJ's congressional arm-twisting, whereas **Bottom-Up Pressure** stresses Birmingham, Washington, and Freedom Summer forced federal action—yet Southern Black **voting rights** remained blocked.
milestones.bridgeToNext: Exactly one month after signing the 1964 Civil Rights Act, Johnson used a disputed naval clash off North Vietnam to win sweeping war powers.

keyTerms.definition: 1964 voter-registration and Freedom School drive in Mississippi where KKK deputies murdered James Chaney, Andrew Goodman, and Michael Schwerner.
Landmark federal statute abolishing legal Jim Crow segregation in public facilities and outlawing employment discrimination via the EEOC.

milestones.title: The Gulf of Tonkin Incident & Congress’s ‘Blank Cheque’ Resolution
milestones.specTag: KT 3.2 • Escalation under Johnson & Gulf of Tonkin Incident (1964)
milestones.enquiryQuestion: How did the August 1964 Gulf of Tonkin incident hand Johnson a blank cheque for war?
milestones.imageCaption: President Lyndon B. Johnson signing the Gulf of Tonkin Resolution into law in August 1964.
milestones.mapCaption: Reference Map: The August 1964 Gulf of Tonkin incident, Operation Rolling Thunder air raids, and March 1965 US Marine landings at Da Nang.
milestones.catalyst: With Saigon's **ARVN** near collapse against **the increasing threat of the Vietcong** and **Barry Goldwater** accusing LBJ of being soft on communism during the 1964 election, US destroyer ***USS Maddox*** patrolled off North Vietnam.
milestones.turningPoint: After North Vietnamese torpedo boats clashed with *Maddox* (**2 Aug 1964**) and stormy radar triggered a **disputed second attack (4 Aug)**, Congress passed the **Gulf of Tonkin Resolution (7 Aug 1964)**—416–0 in the House, **88–2** in the Senate.
milestones.impact: Handed Johnson a legislative **'blank cheque'** to take *'all necessary measures'* in Southeast Asia without a formal declaration of war, paving the way for full-scale American escalation in early 1965.
milestones.bridgeToNext: Before US ground troops landed in Vietnam, growing anger in America's northern ghettos spotlighted Malcolm X's radical alternative to King—cut short by assassination in February 1965.

keyTerms.definition: 2 August clash between North Vietnamese patrol boats and USS Maddox followed by an unverified 4 August radar alert.
7 August 1964 congressional vote authorising President Johnson to use unlimited military force in Vietnam without declaring war.

milestones.title: Malcolm X, The Black Muslims (Nation of Islam) & Assassination
milestones.specTag: KT 2.3 • Malcolm X, Black Muslims, Change of Attitude & Assassination
milestones.enquiryQuestion: Why did Malcolm X and the Black Muslims appeal to northern Black Americans—and how did his views evolve?
milestones.imageCaption: Malcolm X addressing a rally as chief national spokesperson of the Black Muslims (Nation of Islam).
milestones.catalyst: Southern civil rights laws did little for northern urban ghettos facing **de facto segregation**, slum housing, joblessness, and police brutality—fuelling rapid growth in **Elijah Muhammad's Black Muslims (Nation of Islam)**.
milestones.turningPoint: As minister for the **Black Muslims**, **Malcolm X** rejected King's non-violence for Black separatism, pride, and **self-defence (*'by any means necessary'*)**; after his **1964 Mecca pilgrimage**, he embraced interracial brotherhood and founded the **OAAU** before rival Black Muslims **assassinated him (21 Feb 1965)**.
milestones.impact: Q3d Core Debate: **Divisive Extremism** argues separatist rhetoric alienated white allies, whereas **Cultural Empowerment** stresses Malcolm X instilled Black pride, exposed northern ghetto injustice, and inspired **Black Power**.
milestones.bridgeToNext: Two weeks after Malcolm X's assassination in New York, March 1965 brought simultaneous watershed moments in Da Nang, Vietnam and Selma, Alabama.

keyTerms.definition: Islamic Black nationalist movement led by Elijah Muhammad preaching racial separation, self-reliance, and pride in northern cities.
Secular group (OAAU) founded by Malcolm X in 1964 after his Hajj to Mecca softened his stance on working with anti-racist whites.

milestones.title: Operation Rolling Thunder & First US Combat Marines at Da Nang
milestones.specTag: KT 3.2–3.3 • Escalation to Full Air & Ground War (March 1965)
milestones.enquiryQuestion: How did Operation Rolling Thunder and landing Marines at Da Nang Americanise the Vietnam War?
milestones.imageCaption: Combat troops of the 9th US Marine Expeditionary Brigade landing at Red Beach, Da Nang on 8 March 1965.
milestones.catalyst: In **February 1965**, a **Vietcong mortar raid on the US base at Pleiku** killed 8 Americans and wounded 100+, giving Johnson the trigger to escalate using his Tonkin authority.
milestones.turningPoint: On **2 March 1965**, Johnson launched **Operation Rolling Thunder** (3.5 years, **864,000+ tons of bombs** on North Vietnam), and on **8 March 1965**, **3,500 US Marines landed at Da Nang**—beginning **General Westmoreland**'s troop surge to **536,000 by 1968**.
milestones.impact: Crossed the threshold from advisory aid into a massive American conventional war, yet strategic bombing failed to break an agricultural North Vietnam or sever the jungle **Ho Chi Minh Trail**.
milestones.bridgeToNext: One day before US Marines waded ashore at Da Nang, Alabama state troopers clubbed peaceful voting-rights marchers on Selma's Edmund Pettus Bridge.

keyTerms.definition: Sustained three-year US strategic bombing offensive against North Vietnamese industry, transport, and supply depots.
Arrival of 3,500 US combat Marines initially to guard airbases, marking America's entry into direct ground war in Vietnam.

milestones.title: Selma’s ‘Bloody Sunday’ & Passage of the Voting Rights Act (1965)
milestones.specTag: KT 2.2 • Selma Campaign & Voting Rights Act (1965)
milestones.enquiryQuestion: How did televised brutality at Selma produce the transformative Voting Rights Act of 1965?
milestones.imageCaption: Dr Martin Luther King Jr. and civil rights leaders marching from Selma to Montgomery in March 1965 after 'Bloody Sunday'.
milestones.catalyst: In **Selma, Alabama**, Sheriff Jim Clark's intimidation kept **fewer than 2%** of eligible Black residents registered to vote, prompting **King (SCLC)** and **John Lewis (SNCC)** to launch a voting-rights campaign.
milestones.turningPoint: On **7 March 1965 ('Bloody Sunday')**, state troopers clubbed and tear-gassed 600 peaceful marchers on the **Edmund Pettus Bridge** on national TV; Johnson declared *'We shall overcome'* to Congress and signed the **Voting Rights Act on 6 August 1965**.
milestones.impact: Abolished **literacy tests** and dispatched **federal voting examiners** across the Deep South—doubling Southern Black voter registration past **60%** within four years and electing hundreds of Black officials.
milestones.bridgeToNext: While legal disenfranchisement ended in the South, deep-seated guerrilla warfare in Vietnam exposed the fatal limits of high-tech American tactics.

keyTerms.definition: Brutal televised attack by Alabama state troopers with clubs and tear gas against peaceful Selma-to-Montgomery voting marchers.
Federal statute banning literacy tests and sending federal registrars into Southern counties to enforce 15th Amendment voting rights.

milestones.title: Vietcong Guerrilla Tactics vs US Search & Destroy and Chemical Warfare
milestones.specTag: KT 3.3 • Nature of the Conflict in Vietnam (1964–68)
milestones.enquiryQuestion: Why did Search and Destroy, Agent Orange, and napalm fail to defeat Vietcong guerrillas?
milestones.imageCaption: US soldier setting fire to a suspected Vietcong dwelling during a Search and Destroy sweep in January 1966.
milestones.catalyst: Outgunned by US helicopters and B-52s, **Vietcong** fighters fought an asymmetric **guerrilla war**: blending into villages without uniforms, **'hanging onto US belt buckles'**, digging **250km Cu Chi tunnels**, and laying **punji-stick booby traps** (11%+ of US casualties).
milestones.turningPoint: General **Westmoreland** waged attrition via helicopter **Search and Destroy** ('Zippo' raids measured by enemy **body counts**), **20m gallons of Agent Orange** defoliant (*Operation Ranch Hand*), and **napalm** incendiary bombs.
milestones.impact: Q3d Core Debate: **Vietcong Resilience** credits Giap's tunnel/ambush tactics and **Soviet/Chinese aid** down the Ho Chi Minh Trail, whereas **US Tactical Failure** stresses burning huts and chemical weapons alienated the rural **'hearts and minds'** needed for victory.
milestones.bridgeToNext: Meanwhile inside America in 1966, gunshot wounds on a Mississippi highway split the civil rights movement over the electrifying cry of 'Black Power'.
keyAgents: Ho Chi Minh & General Vo Nguyen Giap

keyTerms.definition: Vietcong hit-and-run ambushes, punji booby traps, and multi-level underground tunnel complexes neutralising US air superiority.
Westmoreland's helicopter-borne attrition sweeps burning suspected VC villages ('Zippo raids') and measuring success by body counts.
Toxic chemical defoliant stripping jungle cover and petroleum jelly burning at 1,000°C—inflicting horrific civilian harm.

milestones.title: Stokely Carmichael’s ‘Black Power’ & Founding of the Black Panther Party
milestones.specTag: KT 2.3 • Emergence of Black Power & Methods/Achievements of Black Panthers
milestones.enquiryQuestion: How did Stokely Carmichael and the Black Panthers reshape the struggle from 1966?
milestones.imageCaption: Huey P. Newton, co-founder with Bobby Seale of the Black Panther Party for Self-Defense in Oakland, California in October 1966.
milestones.catalyst: Continued white violence—when a sniper wounded **James Meredith** on his June 1966 *March Against Fear*—and persistent urban poverty convinced younger **SNCC and CORE** activists that non-violent integration was too slow.
milestones.turningPoint: SNCC chairman **Stokely Carmichael** electrified Greenwood, Mississippi in **June 1966** with the chant **'Black Power!'**, and in **October 1966 Huey P. Newton and Bobby Seale** founded the **Black Panther Party** in Oakland with a **Ten-Point Program**, armed police patrols, and **Free Breakfast** clinics.
milestones.impact: Q3d Core Debate: **Movement Fracture** argues armed militancy alienated white moderates and drew lethal **FBI COINTELPRO** raids (Fred Hampton, 1969), whereas **Community Pride** highlights feeding **20,000+ inner-city children** and building lasting cultural dignity.
milestones.bridgeToNext: Growing northern urban desperation had already erupted in Watts days after the 1965 Voting Rights Act—culminating in the deadly 'Long Hot Summer' of 1967.
keyAgents: Black Panther Party (Huey P. Newton & Bobby Seale)

keyTerms.definition: Slogan popularised by SNCC's Stokely Carmichael calling for Black political self-determination, economic control, and cultural pride.
Oakland revolutionary party founded by Huey Newton and Bobby Seale combining armed police monitoring with Free Breakfast and clinic survival programmes.

milestones.title: Watts, King’s Chicago Campaign, 1967 Detroit Riots & The Kerner Report
milestones.specTag: KT 2.4 • Riots of 1965–67, King in the North & Kerner Report (1968)
milestones.enquiryQuestion: Why did northern cities erupt in riots—and what did the 1968 Kerner Report conclude?
milestones.imageCaption: Detroit Free Press front page reporting federal paratroopers deployed during the five-day July 1967 Detroit riot.
milestones.mapCaption: Reference Map: Major urban uprisings of 1965–68 across Watts (Los Angeles), Chicago, Newark, and Detroit.
milestones.catalyst: Five days after the 1965 Voting Rights Act, police brutality sparked the **August 1965 Watts riot** (34 dead, $40m damage), while white mobs stoned **King's 1966 Chicago Freedom Movement** against northern **de facto housing segregation**.
milestones.turningPoint: During the **1967 'Long Hot Summer'**, riots across **100+ cities** peaked in **Newark (26 dead)** and **Detroit (43 dead, federal paratroopers deployed)**; LBJ's **Kerner Report (Feb 1968)** warned America was moving toward *'two societies, one black, one white—separate and unequal'* due to **white institutional racism**.
milestones.impact: Proved Southern voting/public-accommodation laws could not cure northern ghetto unemployment and slum housing—especially as **Vietnam War** spending starved Johnson's Great Society anti-poverty budgets.
milestones.bridgeToNext: The very same month the Kerner Report landed on Johnson's desk, a shock Communist offensive across South Vietnam shattered US war confidence.

keyTerms.definition: Deadly inner-city uprisings triggered by police arrests amid chronic northern ghetto unemployment, slum housing, and racism.
King's northern campaign targeting slum landlords and mortgage redlining, met with brick-throwing white mobs at Marquette Park.
Presidential inquiry blaming white racism for urban riots and warning America was splitting into 'two societies—separate and unequal'.

milestones.title: The Tet Offensive, Walter Cronkite’s Stalemate Verdict & Johnson’s Withdrawal
milestones.specTag: KT 3.3 • Features & Impact of the Tet Offensive (1968)
milestones.enquiryQuestion: Why was the January 1968 Tet Offensive a Vietcong military defeat yet a psychological turning point?
milestones.imageCaption: President Lyndon B. Johnson announcing on 31 March 1968 that he would pause bombing and not seek re-election.
milestones.mapCaption: Reference Map: Simultaneous January 1968 Tet Offensive attacks on over 100 South Vietnamese cities, Hue, Khe Sanh, and the US Embassy in Saigon.
milestones.catalyst: Months after General Westmoreland assured Americans the Vietcong were nearing collapse, **80,000+ VC and NVA fighters** broke the **January 1968 Lunar New Year (Tet) truce**.
milestones.turningPoint: Commandos attacked **100+ southern cities**, held **Hue** for 25 days, and breached the **US Embassy compound in Saigon** for 6 hours on live TV; CBS anchor **Walter Cronkite** declared the war an unwinnable stalemate (Feb), and **Johnson withdrew from the presidential race on 31 March 1968**.
milestones.impact: Although the Vietcong suffered **~50,000 casualties** and failed to spark an urban uprising, Tet blew open the **Credibility Gap**, ended US troop escalation, and forced Washington to open Paris peace talks.
milestones.bridgeToNext: Exactly four days after Johnson's shock televised withdrawal, an assassin's bullet in Memphis struck down Martin Luther King Jr.
keyAgents: Ho Chi Minh & General Vo Nguyen Giap

keyTerms.definition: Massive surprise Communist offensive across 100+ South Vietnamese towns and the Saigon US Embassy during the Tet holiday.
Public distrust between optimistic White House/Pentagon victory claims and nightly colour TV images of bloody stalemate.

milestones.title: Assassination of Martin Luther King Jr. & The Fair Housing Act (1968)
milestones.specTag: KT 2.4 • Assassination of Martin Luther King & Its Impact
milestones.enquiryQuestion: How did Martin Luther King's April 1968 assassination reshape the civil rights movement?
milestones.imageCaption: Dr Martin Luther King Jr. marching in Memphis in support of striking Black sanitation workers days before his assassination on 4 April 1968.
milestones.catalyst: Pivoting toward nationwide economic justice through the **Poor People's Campaign**, **Dr Martin Luther King Jr.** travelled to **Memphis, Tennessee** to back striking Black sanitation workers.
milestones.turningPoint: On **4 April 1968**, white supremacist James Earl Ray shot King dead on the balcony of the **Lorraine Motel**, igniting grief and uprisings across **100+ US cities**; on **11 April**, Congress passed the **Civil Rights Act of 1968 (Fair Housing Act)**.
milestones.impact: Outlawed racial discrimination in selling, renting, or financing homes, yet deprived the movement of its unifying moral leader—leaving Ralph Abernathy's muddy *Resurrection City* camp unable to maintain pre-1968 momentum.
milestones.bridgeToNext: Six months later at the October 1968 Mexico City Olympics, two Black American sprinters broadcast defiant Black Power symbolism around the globe.

keyTerms.definition: Murder of Dr Martin Luther King Jr. at the Lorraine Motel while supporting striking sanitation workers, sparking 100-city riots.
Civil Rights Act of 1968 banning racial discrimination in housing sales, rentals, and mortgages.

milestones.title: 1968 Mexico Olympics Salute & Scale of Civil Rights Progress by 1975
milestones.specTag: KT 2.3–2.4 • 1968 Mexico Olympics & Scale of Progress by 1975
milestones.enquiryQuestion: What did the 1968 Olympic salute symbolize—and how far had civil rights progressed by 1975?
milestones.imageCaption: US sprinters Tommie Smith and John Carlos raising gloved fists in the Black Power salute on the 200m podium at the Mexico City Olympics, 16 October 1968.
milestones.catalyst: Continuing Black poverty and discrimination despite the 1964–68 Acts inspired US 200m medallists **Tommie Smith** (gold) and **John Carlos** (bronze) to stage a human-rights protest before **400m TV viewers**.
milestones.turningPoint: On **16 October 1968** at the **Mexico City Olympics**, Smith and Carlos stood in **black socks** (poverty) and raised **black-gloved fists** during the US anthem (suspended from the Games); into the early **1970s**, courts ordered school **busing** (*Swann*, 1971) and Nixon backed **affirmative action**.
milestones.impact: Q3d Core Debate on **Progress by 1975**: **Transformative Gains** cites abolished Jim Crow, **~1,500+ Black elected officials** (18 in Congress, mayors in Atlanta/LA/Detroit), and a growing middle class; **Incomplete Equality** stresses Black unemployment stayed **double white rates** amid white 'busing' backlash.
milestones.bridgeToNext: Three weeks after Mexico City, Republican Richard Nixon won the November 1968 presidency promising 'peace with honour' in Vietnam.

keyTerms.definition: Black-gloved fist salute by US sprinters Tommie Smith and John Carlos protesting Black poverty and inequality worldwide.

keyTerms.term: De Jure vs De Facto Progress (1975)
keyTerms.definition: Contrast by 1975 between total abolition of Southern legal Jim Crow and persistent economic/housing inequality in northern cities.

milestones.title: The Nixon Doctrine, Vietnamisation & Attacks on Cambodia and Laos
milestones.specTag: KT 3.4 • Changes under Nixon: Vietnamisation & Widening the War
milestones.enquiryQuestion: Why did Nixon introduce Vietnamisation—and why did it fail despite invading Cambodia and Laos?
milestones.imageCaption: South Vietnamese ARVN armoured carriers advancing during the joint US-ARVN incursion into Cambodia in spring 1970.
milestones.mapCaption: Reference Map: Secret US bombing (Operation Menu, 1969) and ground attacks against Ho Chi Minh Trail bases in Cambodia (1970) and Laos (1971).
milestones.catalyst: Seeking **'peace with honour'** without cutting and running, **President Richard Nixon** announced the **Nixon Doctrine (July 1969)**—Asian allies must supply their own ground troops—and **Vietnamisation**.
milestones.turningPoint: While cutting US troops from **543,000 (1969) to ~156,000 (late 1971)**, Nixon secretly bombed Cambodia (*Operation Menu*, 1969), sent US-ARVN troops into **Cambodia (April 1970)**, and backed ARVN's failed **Laos invasion (Feb 1971)** to cut the Ho Chi Minh Trail.
milestones.impact: Vietnamisation failed: **ARVN** troops fled clinging to helicopter skids in Laos without US infantry, while remaining US conscripts suffered collapsing morale, heroin use, combat refusals, and **800+ 'fragging' attacks** on officers.
milestones.bridgeToNext: Instead of calming America, My Lai revelations in late 1969 and Nixon's April 1970 Cambodian invasion triggered the fiercest anti-war storm of the conflict.

keyTerms.definition: 1969 policy withdrawing US ground troops steadily while training and equipping South Vietnam's ARVN to fight the ground war.
Nixon's cross-border offensives aiming to destroy Vietcong/NVA sanctuaries along the Ho Chi Minh Trail—inflaming protest and exposing ARVN weakness.
Demoralised US conscripts rolling fragmentation grenades into officers' tents (>800 incidents) to avoid fatal patrols during withdrawal.

milestones.title: Media, Draft Protest, The My Lai Massacre & Kent State Shootings (1970)
milestones.specTag: KT 4.1 • Growth of Opposition: TV, Draft, My Lai & Kent State
milestones.enquiryQuestion: How did TV, the draft, My Lai revelations, and Kent State fuel mass anti-war opposition?
milestones.imageCaption: Armed Ohio National Guardsmen advancing on student anti-war protesters at Kent State University on 4 May 1970.
milestones.mapCaption: Investigative Diagram: Positions of Ohio National Guardsmen and unarmed students during the 4 May 1970 Kent State shootings.
milestones.catalyst: Uncensored **'Living Room War' TV** and an unequal **draft system** (college deferments spared affluent youths while working-class and Black soldiers bore heavy casualties; **Muhammad Ali** refused induction) built **student movement** protests (**Nov 1969 Moratorium: 500,000** in D.C.).
milestones.turningPoint: In **Nov 1969**, journalist Seymour Hersh exposed the **March 1968 My Lai Massacre** (>500 unarmed villagers killed under **Lt. William Calley**, convicted 1971); days after Nixon invaded Cambodia, **Ohio National Guardsmen shot 4 unarmed students dead at Kent State University (4 May 1970)**.
milestones.impact: Triggered a **4-million-student strike shutting 400+ US colleges**, drove veterans (**VVAW**, April 1971) to hurl medals at the Capitol, and pushed Congress to repeal the Gulf of Tonkin Resolution.
milestones.bridgeToNext: Yet campus strikes and flag-burning provoked an equally fierce patriotic backlash from Nixon's 'silent majority' and blue-collar 'hard hats'.

keyTerms.definition: Selective Service conscription whose class-skewed college deferments sparked draft-card burnings and SDS campus rallies.
March 1968 slaughter of >500 unarmed Vietnamese civilians exposed in Nov 1969; Lt. Calley was the sole soldier convicted (commuted by Nixon).
Killing of four unarmed students in Ohio by National Guardsmen during Cambodian invasion protests, paralysing US universities.

milestones.title: Support for the War: Nixon’s ‘Silent Majority’, Hard Hat Riots & 1972 Landslide
milestones.specTag: KT 4.2 • Fear of Communism, ‘Hard Hats’ & ‘Silent Majority’
milestones.enquiryQuestion: Why did millions of Americans in the 'silent majority' and 'hard hats' continue backing Nixon?
milestones.imageCaption: President Richard Nixon in the Oval Office beside stacks of supportive public telegrams after his 3 November 1969 'Silent Majority' speech.
milestones.mapCaption: Reference Map: Nixon's 49-state presidential landslide (520–17 electoral votes) over anti-war Democrat George McGovern in November 1972.
milestones.catalyst: Millions of older, suburban, and blue-collar Americans driven by **the fear of communism**, Cold War patriotism, and anger at privileged student draft-dodgers backed Nixon's **3 November 1969 'silent majority' speech** (77% approval).
milestones.turningPoint: Four days after Kent State (**8 May 1970**), hundreds of New York construction workers—**the 'hard hats'**—attacked anti-war student marchers on Wall Street and were welcomed at the White House; campaigning on Vietnamisation and law-and-order, Nixon won **49 of 50 states in November 1972**.
milestones.impact: Q3d Core Debate: Demonstrates that vocal campus protest never spoke for all Americans—**Middle America** rejected immediate humiliating defeat even while welcoming troop pullouts.
milestones.bridgeToNext: Armed with his November 1972 landslide, Nixon unleashed massive B-52 Christmas bombings to force a Paris peace exit—just as Watergate began unravelling his presidency.

keyTerms.definition: Nixon's appeal to law-abiding, patriotic suburban and working-class voters who did not join street protests and backed 'peace with honour'.
Pro-war blue-collar construction workers who assaulted student protesters in Manhattan and rallied in support of Nixon.

milestones.title: Pentagon Papers, Christmas Bombings, Paris Peace Agreement (1973) & Watergate
milestones.specTag: KT 4.3 • Peace Negotiations, Paris Peace Agreement (1973) & War Costs
milestones.enquiryQuestion: How did the January 1973 Paris Peace Agreement, War Powers Act, and Watergate isolate Saigon?
milestones.imageCaption: US Secretary of State William P. Rogers signing the Paris Peace Agreement on 27 January 1973 to end direct US combat in Vietnam.
milestones.catalyst: Daniel Ellsberg's **June 1971 Pentagon Papers** leak exposed decades of White House deception, while **Henry Kissinger**'s secret Paris talks with **Le Duc Tho** stalled in late 1972 when Saigon's President Thieu balked at terms.
milestones.turningPoint: Nixon ordered **11 days of B-52 'Christmas Bombings' (Linebacker II, Dec 1972)** on Hanoi/Haiphong before all sides signed the **Paris Peace Agreement (27 Jan 1973)**: **ceasefire in place**, **591 US POWs freed**, final US troops out (**29 March 1973**), while **150,000 NVA troops stayed in the South**.
milestones.impact: Ended America's combat role (**58,220 US dead**, 300,000 wounded, **$168bn** spent), while Congress overrode a **Watergate-crippled** Nixon to pass the **Nov 1973 War Powers Act** before **Nixon resigned over Watergate (Aug 1974)**—guaranteeing no US air return.
milestones.bridgeToNext: Seeing Congress slash Saigon's aid and President Gerald Ford legally bound after Watergate, North Vietnam launched its final offensive in spring 1975.

keyTerms.definition: Heavy 11-day US B-52 'Christmas Bombing' of Hanoi and Haiphong forcing final signature of the Paris Peace Agreement.
Treaty ending US military involvement and freeing US POWs while leaving ~150,000 North Vietnamese soldiers inside South Vietnam.
November 1973 law curbing presidential war powers alongside the Watergate scandal (Nixon resigned Aug 1974), preventing US re-intervention.

milestones.title: The Fall of Saigon (30 April 1975) & Reasons for US Failure in Vietnam
milestones.specTag: KT 4.4 • Fall of Saigon & Strengths/Weaknesses Explaining US Failure
milestones.enquiryQuestion: Why did the world's strongest military superpower fail to prevent Communist victory in Vietnam?
milestones.imageCaption: Evacuees boarding a US Marine helicopter during Operation Frequent Wind on the eve of the Fall of Saigon, 29–30 April 1975.
milestones.mapCaption: Reference Map: North Vietnam's 1975 Spring Offensive sweeping south to capture Saigon on 30 April 1975.
milestones.catalyst: Starved of fuel, spare parts, and US air cover after post-1973 congressional aid cuts, corrupt **ARVN** divisions collapsed rapidly when General **Van Tien Dung** launched North Vietnam's **January–April 1975 Spring Offensive**.
milestones.turningPoint: On **29–30 April 1975**, US helicopters evacuated 7,000+ Americans and allies from rooftops (**Operation Frequent Wind**) hours before North Vietnamese tanks crashed through Saigon's Independence Palace gates (**Fall of Saigon**), reunifying Vietnam under Communist rule.
milestones.impact: Q3d Core Debate on **Why the USA Failed**: **North Vietnamese/VC Strengths** (unbreakable nationalist will, guerrilla tactics, **Ho Chi Minh Trail**, **Russian & Chinese arms**) vs **US Military Failures** (Search & Destroy/chemicals losing peasant hearts & minds, 12-month conscripts) & **Domestic Anti-War/Media Opposition**.
milestones.bridgeToNext: From Brown and Geneva in 1954 to Saigon in 1975, twenty-one years of conflict dismantled legal Jim Crow at home while shattering Cold War certainty abroad.
keyAgents: Ho Chi Minh & General Vo Nguyen Giap

keyTerms.definition: Capture of South Vietnam's capital by North Vietnamese tanks after Operation Frequent Wind, reunifying Vietnam as a Communist state.
Billions in Soviet SAM missiles, artillery, trucks, and Chinese weapons shipped down the Ho Chi Minh Trail to sustain Hanoi and the VC.
Inability of corrupt Saigon regimes and destructive US tactics (Search & Destroy, napalm, Agent Orange) to win rural Vietnamese loyalty.
